samples.summary: A repeated `?state=` query parameter makes the callback throw a TypeError (500) instead of the intended 400/redirect
samples.evidence: `verifyCallbackState` does `stateToken?.startsWith(WEB_STATE_PREFIX)`. Nest's `@Query('state')` hands back `string[]` when Express parses `?state=a&state=b`, and arrays have no `.startsWith` → `TypeError: stateToken.startsWith is not a function`, surfacing as an unhandled 500 (and skipping `takeStateCookie`, so neither state cookie is cleared). The previous code only did `this.cliAuthStore.consumeState(stateToken)`, which returned `undefined` for an array and produced the intended 400. The new type narrowing assumes a string that the framework does not guarantee.

samples.summary: `ERROR_MESSAGES[error]` resolves Object.prototype keys, so `?error=toString` renders a function instead of the fallback message
samples.evidence: `ERROR_MESSAGES` is a plain object literal, so `ERROR_MESSAGES["toString"]`/`"constructor"`/`"valueOf"`/`"hasOwnProperty"` return inherited functions. `ERROR_MESSAGES[error] ?? FALLBACK_ERROR` therefore does NOT fall back for those values — the `??` sees a non-nullish function — and React is handed a function as a child ("Functions are not valid as a React child"), showing an empty alert box instead of the fallback text. `error` comes straight from `searchParams.get("error")`, i.e. fully attacker/user controlled. `Object.hasOwn(ERROR_MESSAGES, error)` or a `Map`/`Object.create(null)` fixes it.

samples.summary: The single-use `/launch/<token>` redirect can be consumed by a non-browser fetch, leaving the real browser with a 404 and the login hanging for the full five minutes
samples.evidence: `launchTarget = undefined` after the first GET to `/launch/<token>`, so exactly one request may follow the redirect. Anything that touches the URL before (or instead of) the user's actual page load — a browser that probes the URL, an OS/handler that pre-resolves it, a link scanner/AV proxy, or the URL being opened twice by `open` on some platforms — burns the token; the browser then receives `404 Not found` with no message telling the user what happened, and `waitForCallback()` blocks for `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS` (now 5 minutes, up from 30s) before reporting a generic timeout. There is no fallback path (the announced URL is the authorization URL, not the launch URL, so it only helps if the user reads the TTY/file notice).

samples.summary: `loginErrorUrl` produces a relative, backend-local URL when `FRONTEND_URL` is unset, redirecting the user to a 404 on the API host
samples.evidence: `const base = (this.configService.get<string>('FRONTEND_URL') ?? '').replace(/\/$/, '')` yields `''`, so the redirect target is `/login?error=login_state` — a same-origin path on the backend, which has no `/login` route. The success path uses `this.configService.get('FRONTEND_URL')!` (non-null assertion), so the codebase elsewhere assumes it is always set; here the `?? ''` silently degrades to a broken redirect rather than failing loudly.

samples.summary: A failed CLI callback renders raw JSON 400 in the user's browser, contrary to the comment claiming the CLI reads it
samples.evidence: The catch only converts `UnauthorizedException` into a redirect; `verifyCallbackState`'s CLI branch throws `BadRequestException`, which propagates and is rendered as a JSON body. `GET /auth/github/callback` is a top-level navigation in the *user's browser* (GitHub redirects the browser there; the CLI is only reached by the subsequent 127.0.0.1 redirect), so the comment "its callback is read by the CLI, not by a person" is factually wrong and the person sees an unactionable JSON error page.

samples.summary: Two concurrent browser logins in one browser overwrite each other's `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie, so the first tab's callback is refused
samples.evidence: `issueLoginCookie(context, OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE)` writes one fixed-name cookie per browser start. The class comment fixes exactly this collision for CLI-vs-web by using separate names, but web-vs-web is unaddressed: opening the sign-in link in two tabs (or navigating back and clicking again) makes the second start overwrite the binding, and the first tab's callback lands on `/login?error=login_state` with no visible cause — the same failure mode the comment calls "a login that fails for a reason no one can see."

samples.summary: A browser that does not persist the confirm cookie loops on the CLI consent page forever with no error
samples.evidence: `hasConfirmation` is a pure double-submit check against `CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE`. If the cookie is not stored — e.g. `secureCookies()` returns true (NODE_ENV=production) while the origin is plain http, so the `__Host-`/`Secure` cookie is dropped by the browser — every click on "Continue sign-in" re-enters the unconfirmed branch, re-renders the interstitial and re-issues a new token. The user sees the same page indefinitely with no diagnostic, and the CLI times out.

samples.summary: A successful-but-empty download reports the misleading message `HTTP 200`
samples.evidence: The guard is `if (!res.ok || !res.bytes)`, but the fallback passed to `backendErrorEnvelope` is unconditionally `{ code: 'HTTP_ERROR', message: `HTTP ${res.status}` }`. When `res.ok` is true and `bytes` is missing/empty the user gets `{"error":{"code":"HTTP_ERROR","message":"HTTP 200"}}`, which states the opposite of what happened.

finding.summary: The single-use `/launch/<token>` redirect can be consumed by a non-browser fetch, leaving the real browser with a 404 and the login hanging for the full five minutes
finding.evidence: `launchTarget = undefined` after the first GET to `/launch/<token>`, so exactly one request may follow the redirect. Anything that touches the URL before (or instead of) the user's actual page load — a browser that probes the URL, an OS/handler that pre-resolves it, a link scanner/AV proxy, or the URL being opened twice by `open` on some platforms — burns the token; the browser then receives `404 Not found` with no message telling the user what happened, and `waitForCallback()` blocks for `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS` (now 5 minutes, up from 30s) before reporting a generic timeout. There is no fallback path (the announced URL is the authorization URL, not the launch URL, so it only helps if the user reads the TTY/file notice).

verdict.reason: The mechanism is present exactly as quoted (login.ts:361-384 spends launchTarget on first GET and 404s thereafter; login.ts:323 sets a 5-minute timeout with a generic message at login.ts:455-470), but it is not a blocking correctness defect. (a) There is no logic error: single-use spend-on-first-read is the specified invariant (login.ts:333-338, login.ts:62-69, docs/design/cli.md:271-273) and the handler implements it correctly; no wrong condition, missing guard crash, async mistake, data loss, or leak (timer/server closed in the finally at login.ts:77-82). (b) The finding's decisive consequence claim -- that there is no fallback -- is inaccurate: login.ts:71 calls announceLoginUrl(oauthUrl) unconditionally, before waitForCallback(), and announceLoginUrl (login.ts:211-242) always emits a recovery channel (stderr when TTY, else an 0600 login-url.txt whose path is printed, else an --api-key message). That announced URL carries port, nonce and code_challenge (login.ts:56-59), so visiting it completes the same login into the same listener -- a working recovery, printed before the wait starts. (c) No in-repo caller burns the token: armLaunch has a single call site (login.ts:70) feeding openBrowser, which spawns the opener once (login.ts:188-196), and the 32-byte token is unguessable, so external scanners/proxies cannot address it. Worst case is a stale 404 tab plus a re-run -- a UX/robustness trade-off, not data loss, a crash, or a broken core flow.

finding.summary: CLI login's 30-second callback timeout now has to cover a mandatory human consent click as well as GitHub OAuth
finding.evidence: `startCallbackServer` still arms `setTimeout(..., 30_000)` from the moment the server starts (login.ts:436-451), and the timer is started *before* `armLaunch`/`openBrowser` even run. The change inserts a new blocking human step into that window: `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` no longer redirects a `mode=cli` start to GitHub at all — it renders the consent interstitial (github-auth.guard.ts:226-235) and waits for the user to read it and click "Continue sign-in". So the 30 s must now cover browser launch + interstitial read + click + GitHub round trip, where previously it only covered browser launch + GitHub. The backend's own bindings live 5 minutes (`STATE_COOKIE_MAX_AGE_MS`, state TTL in cli-auth.store.ts:70) and the CLI even prints "it expires in 5 minutes" (login.ts:231), so the two ends disagree by an order of magnitude and the CLI will abort a login the server still considers valid, printing the misleading "Login timed out. Try again with `wafflebase login`."

verdict.reason: The claimed 30-second timeout does not exist in this repository. `startCallbackServer` arms its only setTimeout with `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS` (login.ts:470), which is defined as `5 * 60 * 1000` at login.ts:323; there is no `30_000`/`30000` literal anywhere in packages/cli/src (the sole `30000` in the package is an unrelated Vitest test timeout at test/docs-export.test.ts:184). The reviewer's cited lines 436-451 are the success-page HTML/CSS template, not timer code. The alleged order-of-magnitude disagreement also does not exist: the CLI's 5 minutes matches STATE_COOKIE_MAX_AGE_MS (github-auth.guard.ts:49) and the store's state TTL (cli-auth.store.ts:70), and matches the CLI's own "expires in 5 minutes" message (login.ts:231); a test pins the value (test/login-callback.test.ts:119). The finding's other premises are true — the guard does render a consent interstitial for mode=cli (github-auth.guard.ts:279-288) and the timer is armed before armLaunch/openBrowser — but with a 300-second budget the few milliseconds of listen/spawn before arming is not a correctness defect.

finding.summary: A `mode=cli` start with an out-of-range port silently downgrades into a full browser login instead of being refused
finding.evidence: `if (Number.isInteger(portNum) && portNum >= 1024 && portNum <= 65535)` (line 202) wraps the whole CLI branch. When the port fails the range check the code falls through to line 249, which mints a *web* `state`, and the callback then takes the browser branch and issues real session cookies plus a redirect to `FRONTEND_URL` (auth.controller.ts:244-248). This contradicts the stated invariant applied to `nonce`/`code_challenge` a few lines below ("Missing and malformed are the same failure ... Refusing costs an upgrade; accepting costs the account") — a malformed port is silently accepted as a different flow. Observable effect: `wafflebase login` against a bad port hangs to the 30 s timeout with "Login timed out" while the user's browser has quietly been logged into the web app. The controller's later `if (port < 1024 || port > 65535) throw new BadRequestException('Invalid CLI port')` (auth.controller.ts:231) is now unreachable dead code for the same reason.

verdict.reason: The finding's central evidence is fabricated relative to this repo. It claims github-auth.guard.ts has `if (Number.isInteger(portNum) && portNum >= 1024 && portNum <= 65535)` wrapping the whole CLI branch, letting a bad port fall through to the web flow. The actual code at github-auth.guard.ts:256-259 is the inverse — a negated early-throw guard: `if (!Number.isInteger(portNum) || portNum < 1024 || portNum > 65535) { throw new BadRequestException('Missing or invalid port'); }`. An out-of-range/non-integer/missing port therefore throws 400 before any state is minted and can never reach the web-state fallback (github-auth.guard.ts:301-307) or the browser cookie/redirect branch (auth.controller.ts:245-249). A repo-wide grep shows line 257 is the sole occurrence of this logic; there is no other copy. The comment at github-auth.guard.ts:250-255 explicitly describes the fall-through behavior as what "an unusable port used to do", i.e. the very thing this code removed, and the port is held to the same refuse-on-malformed rule as nonce (262) and code_challenge (272). The secondary claim that auth.controller.ts:232 is now unreachable dead code fails with it: that check is redundant defense-in-depth over a store value that only ever originates from the already-validated portNum passed to CliAuthStore.createState (github-auth.guard.ts:291-297), and redundant validation is not a correctness defect regardless. Tests at github-auth.guard.spec.ts:163,191 assert the refusal semantics the finding says are absent.
